title: A set of points S is Euclidean Ramsey if, for every k, there exists an N so that every k-coloring of Euclidean N-space c
exact_target: Call a finite point set $S$ Euclidean Ramsey if, for every finite number of colors, some Euclidean dimension has the property that every coloring of the whole space contains a monochromatic isometric copy of $S$. Must every finite set that lies on a sphere be Euclidean Ramsey? The four-point subsets of a circle are included.
